clinicalPearls: Blue-grey dermal melanocytic pigmentation over the shoulder, supraclavicular, scapular and deltoid region, following the posterior supraclavicular and lateral brachial cutaneous nerves
Analogous to naevus of Ota but affecting the shoulder girdle rather than the face, and without ocular involvement
May coexist with an ipsilateral naevus of Ota in the same individual
The pigment is dermal, so it shows no Wood-lamp accentuation and topical agents are ineffective
More common in Asian populations and in females
Pigment-specific laser is the mainstay of treatment where cosmetic improvement is desired
Malignant transformation is very rare but has been reported, so persistent change warrants review
reference.pathophysiology: As in naevus of Ota, the lesion results from melanocytes of neural crest origin that fail to complete their migration to the epidermis and remain within the dermis. These dermal melanocytes produce melanin whose deep location scatters light to give the blue-grey colour. The distribution corresponds to the shoulder-girdle cutaneous nerves rather than the trigeminal territory.
additionalInvestigations: Dermoscopy to confirm the dermal melanocytic pattern
Full skin examination to detect a coexisting naevus of Ota
Wood-lamp examination to confirm the pigment is dermal
Biopsy of any nodular or atypical area to exclude melanoma
redFlags: Development of a nodule or focal change suggesting melanoma
Rapid growth or ulceration within the lesion
New symptoms such as bleeding or persistent tenderness
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign and persists lifelong if untreated, with good cosmetic response to pigment-specific laser and only a very small risk of malignant change.
pitfalls: Mistaking the blue-grey patch for a persistent bruise
Attempting to treat dermal pigment with topical lightening agents
Failing to look for a coexisting naevus of Ota
Overlooking a rare melanoma developing within the naevus
